source: Sweller (1994) Cognitive load theory, learning difficulty, and instructional design
finding: Defines intrinsic load by element interactivity. Elements that must be learned at the same time because they interact give high load. Elements that can be learned one after another give low load. Total load is intrinsic plus extraneous.
numbers: No experiment in this paper. It is a theory paper with a counting method and worked examples.
quote: The primary determinant of intrinsic cognitive load is element interactivity.
limits: Theory paper. Intrinsic load is called constant for a given area, a claim later contested (see a21).
agent_relevance: Supplies the definition behind the S0 gate: difficulty is about how many parts must be held in relation at once, not how long or large the task is.

source: Sweller (1994) Cognitive load theory, learning difficulty, and instructional design
finding: Worked count of interacting elements. Multiplying out a denominator (a/b = c to a = cb) has 5 interacting elements. A foreign-language noun pair has a count of 1.
numbers: 5 elements for the algebra step (multiply left by b; same on right; new equation ab/b = cb; cancel b; a = cb). Count of 1 for a vocabulary item.
limits: Count depends on the learner. For an expert with an automated schema the algebra step is 1 element. For a novice without the first schema it is 6 or more. Sweller says a learner-independent measure is unobtainable.
agent_relevance: The count is relative to the solver. For an agent, the unit is what the model can treat as one chunk (a known tool, a known pattern). O3 should count after chunking, not before.

source: Sweller (1994) Cognitive load theory, learning difficulty, and instructional design
finding: Paired-associate and vocabulary learning is the extreme of low interactivity. It can be hard because of the amount of information, but not because of interactivity. Anatomy terms are another example.
numbers: No numbers. Examples: paired associates, second-language vocabulary, anatomy terminology.
limits: Vocabulary stops being low interactivity once it must be used in syntax. Sweller notes this himself.
agent_relevance: Separates two kinds of hardness: many independent items (needs serial handling, memory aids, retrieval) versus few items that interlock (needs decomposition or a schema). The agent should route these differently.

source: Sweller (1994) Cognitive load theory, learning difficulty, and instructional design
finding: Prediction: extraneous load (split attention, redundancy, no worked example) hurts only when intrinsic load is high. With low element interactivity the same effects may vanish because total load stays under capacity.
numbers: No new data in this paper. Sweller says initial data collected strongly support it.
quote: So none of the cognitive load effects may occur if element interactivity is low.
limits: Stated as a hypothesis here. Tested by Sweller and Chandler (1994) and Chandler and Sweller (1996), see a07 and a08.
agent_relevance: Supports a cost rule: do not spend scaffold effort (decompose, restate, clean the context) on items with few interacting parts. This matches guardrails G7 and G12.

source: Sweller (1994) Cognitive load theory, learning difficulty, and instructional design
finding: Explains why some material needs to be understood and other material only learned. Failing to learn some interacting elements is called a failure of understanding. Failing to learn one independent element is just forgetting.
numbers: Example: ending with a/b = cb instead of a = cb counts as not understood.
limits: Philosophical claim. No test.
agent_relevance: A partial solution that satisfies some constraints but not their joint interaction is the typical failure on high-interactivity items. Checks should test the joint constraint, not each part alone (links to G3).

source: Sweller (1994), citing Halford, Maybery and Bain (1986) and Maybery, Bain and Halford (1986): transitive inference
finding: Independent early evidence that interacting elements load working memory. In 'a is larger than b; b is larger than c; which is largest', integrating the two premises is the heaviest step, measured by a secondary task.
numbers: Numbers not given in Sweller 1994. See a19 for the Halford 1998 account of the same studies.
limits: Seen only as cited in Sweller (1994) and Halford et al. (1998). Original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: The load peaks at the integration step, not at reading. An agent should expect errors at the join of premises, and place checks there.

source: Sweller and Chandler (1994) Why some material is difficult to learn, Cognition and Instruction 12(3), 185-233
finding: Four experiments on learning to use computer equipment or procedures with and without the equipment present. Redesigning to remove split attention helped with high element interactivity material and did not help with low element interactivity material.
numbers: Exact means and N not available to me. Abstract-level only (seen via search summary and Sweller 1994 and 2002 summaries).
limits: Not opened. Full text paywalled. Numbers must be pulled by another route before use.
agent_relevance: First direct test of the element interactivity effect. Treat the effect as supported but get the numbers before quoting.

source: Chandler and Sweller (1996) Cognitive load while learning to use a computer program, Applied Cognitive Psychology 10
finding: Split-attention and redundancy effects appeared with high element interactivity material and disappeared with low element interactivity material (as summarized by Sweller).
numbers: Numbers not available to me.
limits: Seen only through Sweller's summary in the Visualisation and Instructional Design paper (a09).
agent_relevance: Same as a07. Second source for the claim that scaffold benefits depend on item interactivity.

source: Sweller (c. 2002) Visualisation and instructional design (conference paper, UNSW)
finding: Names the 'element interactivity effect': split-attention, redundancy and modality effects occur with high element interactivity material and vanish with low. Cites Chandler and Sweller 1996, Sweller and Chandler 1994, Tindall-Ford et al. 1997 (modality), Marcus et al. 1996 (diagrams vs text).
numbers: No numbers given. Review of four studies, all reported as showing the interaction.
quote: The effects may only be obtainable using high element interactivity material.
limits: Date inferred from the references (latest 2001). Secondary summary by Sweller himself, so it is not independent of the original authors.
agent_relevance: The 'cognitive load effects depend on complexity' idea is an interaction effect, and interaction effects are what a scaffold gate has to detect.

source: Cooper, Tindall-Ford, Chandler and Sweller (2001) Learning by imagining, as summarized in Sweller (c. 2002)
finding: Telling learners to imagine a procedure beat telling them to study it, but only for learners with enough knowledge to hold all interacting elements in working memory. For complete novices the result reversed and study won.
numbers: Numbers not given in the page I read.
limits: Seen via Sweller's summary only. Original not opened.
agent_relevance: A sign flip with expertise: the same prompt trick (imagine, self-run) helps when the problem fits in working memory and hurts when it does not. Chen et al. (2016, a14) frame the same flip as expertise reversal.

source: Leahy, Chandler and Sweller (2003) When auditory presentations should and should not be a component of multimedia instruction, Applied Cognitive Psychology 17, 401-418
finding: Experiment 1, N=48 Year 5 pupils (24 per group), temperature line graph. Audio plus diagram beat diagram plus written text only on questions with many interacting elements, with no difference on questions with few.
numbers: Mean percent correct, low then high interactivity. Audio/visual: 73.33 and 34.26 (SD 24.79, 28.73). Visual only: 74.17 and 15.74 (SD 21.65, 20.17). Group x interactivity: F(1,46)=6.62, p=.013. High-interactivity simple effect t(46)=2.58, p=.014. Low: t(46)=0.124, p=.902.
limits: Questions were classed low or high by the authors' own element count (8-element questions 1,2,4,5,12 were the ones that differed). Counts are estimates. Single school, short test.
agent_relevance: Direct numbers for the claim that the same scaffold change shows its gain only on high-interactivity items.

source: Leahy, Chandler and Sweller (2003), Experiment 1 question-level counts
finding: Per-question counts follow the element count. On the 8-element questions the audio/visual group got 8, 9, 8, 9 and 10 right out of 24 versus 1, 2, 3, 3 and 3 for visual only. On 1-element questions the groups were close (18 vs 19, 21 vs 23).
numbers: Questions 1,2,4,5,12 (count 8): A/V 8,9,8,9,10 vs visual-only 1,2,3,3,3 out of 24. Q7, Q8 (count 1): A/V 18, 21 vs visual-only 19, 23.
limits: Q9 and Q10 (count 7) showed no significant difference (9 vs 7, 8 vs 7), so the effect is not smooth in the count. Only 8-element questions differed. Looks like a threshold, not a line.
agent_relevance: Hints at a threshold near 7 to 8 interacting elements for these children. Treat any numeric threshold as population-specific.

source: Leahy, Chandler and Sweller (2003), Experiment 2 (redundancy), N=30
finding: When the audio only repeated text already in the diagram, the audio group did worse. The diagram-only group studied for 62.3 s against 135 s of audio for the other group, and still scored higher.
numbers: Group effect F(1,28)=9.18, p=.005. Interaction F(1,28)=5.56, p=.026. High-interactivity simple effect t(28)=3.03, p=.006; low t(28)=2.29, p=.030. From Table 4 counts I compute (not in paper): diagram-only 78/105 right on the 7 high-count questions (74%) versus 42/105 (40%) for audio; on the 7 low-count questions 99/105 (94%) versus 86/105 (82%).
limits: Two pupil groups of 15 (30 total). The low-interactivity gap was also significant, so the pattern is larger on high, not absent on low. The Table 3 values did not extract cleanly, so I used counts.
agent_relevance: Redundant narration or restating the same content hurt more on hard items. Supports not adding restated context by default (G11) and testing any restatement operator at equal tokens (G7).

source: Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller (2016) When instructional guidance is needed, Educational and Developmental Psychologist 33(2), 149-162
finding: 2x2 geometry experiment, Year 6 pupils in Chengdu. Generation beat reading for low-interactivity formulae (about 1 element). For high-interactivity composite-shape area problems (about 6 interacting elements) the direction reversed but the worked-example effect was not significant.
numbers: N=47 after 3 dropped (22 high guidance, 25 low). Means, low-interactivity then high: high guidance 71.4 (SD 20.15) and 90.9 (10.08); low guidance 80.9 (13.82) and 85.6 (16.09). Interaction F(1,45)=5.16, p=.028. Generation effect t(46)=-2.02, p=.025 one-tailed, d=.57. Worked example t(46)=1.60, p=.06 one-tailed, d=.46.
limits: The key worked-example effect was not significant. Interaction is carried partly by a non-significant simple effect. Tests differed between the two levels, so the main effect of interactivity is not interpretable. Same pupils took both phases 4 hours apart. One-tailed tests. Authors also say it could be an expertise reversal case.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete count (about 6 interacting elements) as the high-interactivity task, and a rule for the agent: give full guidance (worked steps) on high-interactivity items, let it generate on low-interactivity ones.

source: Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller (2016): how element interactivity was counted
finding: Shows a transparent counting recipe. Each familiar formula symbol is one element. For the rhombus plus trapezium figure: recognise rhombus (1), recognise trapezium (2), total area (3), addition (4), the two areas (5 and 6), giving about 6.
numbers: About 6 elements for the worked-example task and 1 for the formula-recall task.
limits: Counting is by the authors' judgement, not validated against a second rater. Learner expertise is assumed (rhombus and trapezium areas are already single chunks for Year 6).
agent_relevance: A template for how O3 could score a sub-problem: list the objects, relations and operations that must be held together, after merging known chunks.

source: Sweller (2010) Element interactivity and intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load, Educational Psychology Review 22, 123-138
finding: Argues element interactivity is the defining mechanism of intrinsic load and also underlies extraneous load. Germane load is redefined as working memory resources devoted to the intrinsic load, so it is tied to element interactivity too.
numbers: None retrieved. Abstract-level only.
limits: Not opened. Paywalled. Only the abstract and secondary quotes were seen.
agent_relevance: Collapses three loads into one measure (interacting elements, split into those the task needs and those the presentation adds). A single count may be enough for a gate.

source: Halford, Wilson and Phillips (1998) Processing capacity defined by relational complexity, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21, 803-865
finding: Formal measure of the same idea: complexity is the number of interacting variables (arguments of a relation) that must be represented in parallel. Unary, binary, ternary, quaternary. Human adults have a soft limit near one quaternary relation (four related variables).
numbers: Quaternary example: proportion a/b = c/d. Neural-net model: about five units can be active so one quaternary relation fits (symbol plus four arguments). Children: ternary relations by median age about 5 years.
quote: Studies of working memory limits suggest that there is a soft limit corresponding to the parallel processing of one quaternary relation.
limits: A soft limit, with errors rising gracefully. Task complexity is the complexity of the most complex step, not the number of steps. Strategy dependent: measure with the least demanding strategy available. Many commentaries disputed the exact number.
agent_relevance: A principled bound for O3: split until no step needs more than about four things bound together. Also shows that many steps in a row is not hard if each step is simple (matches CogniLoad length vs difficulty results).

source: Halford et al. (1998): segmentation and conceptual chunking
finding: Two ways to handle tasks beyond the limit. Segmentation breaks the task into parts that fit and are processed one after the other. Conceptual chunking collapses a structure into fewer dimensions but loses access to the inner relations.
numbers: Not numeric. Example: 'five days after the day before yesterday is Friday' is hard because many elements are related in the first clause.
limits: Cost of chunking: some relational information becomes inaccessible. Segmentation only works if the parts really can be processed serially (transitive inference cannot be split into binary parts without loss, shown in section 2.2).
agent_relevance: These are the same two moves as O3 decompose (segmentation) and compress or summarize (chunking). Note the cost of chunking: a summary hides relations. G2 should apply.

source: Halford et al. (1998): premise integration in transitive inference
finding: Maybery et al. (1986) used segmented presentation. The load peaked when the second premise had to be integrated with the first, which is a ternary step, and not at premise reading, which is binary. Earlier models that counted negatives did not predict this.
numbers: No numeric values retrieved. Qualitative: the integration step shows the highest cost.
limits: Reported inside a review, secondary account of the original.
agent_relevance: Peak load is at the join. For multi-hop questions, put the verification where the premises are combined.

source: de Jong (2010) Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought, Instructional Science 38, 105-134
finding: Critique of the intrinsic load idea. Difficulty is not set by element count and interactivity alone. Same element count can differ in difficulty (Tower of Hanoi variants), changing ontological category is hard regardless of count, and negative or ambiguous relations add difficulty.
numbers: Klahr and Robinson (1981): all-pegs-occupied Hanoi was harder for children than standard Hanoi with the same number of moves. Chi (1992, 2005) on ontological category change.
limits: A review and argument, not new data. Written in 2010; the theory has since moved (Sweller 2010, a16).
agent_relevance: Warns that the count of parts is only one axis. Conflicting (negative) relations and category mistakes need their own flags in the S0 gate.

source: de Jong (2010) on whether intrinsic load can be changed
finding: CLT texts say intrinsic load is fixed and cannot be changed by instruction. Yet sequencing (simple to complex), part-whole training and whole-part focus are all described in the same literature as ways to control intrinsic load. Van Merrienboer and Sweller (2005) call both consistent with CLT.
numbers: Sources named: Ayres 2006 'fixed and innate'; Sweller et al. 1998 p. 262; Pollock et al. 2002 isolated-elements-first design.
limits: Terminology conflict, not an empirical failure. The effective load on the learner can be changed by splitting the task even if the content's interactivity cannot.
agent_relevance: Exactly what O3 does. The task is not simpler, but the agent never holds all interacting elements at once. Pollock et al. (2002) is the main evidence for it in humans; a follow-up should open it.

source: de Jong (2010) on measurement
finding: The one-item mental effort rating has no stable meaning. The same score is called high in one study and low in another, and does not separate intrinsic from extraneous load.
numbers: Example: the best-performing group in Pollock et al. reported higher load than the worst-performing group in Kablan and Erden. Rikers read a 4.38 to 5.63 rating on a 9-point scale as high.
limits: Review of study-level inconsistencies, no meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Subjective difficulty ratings (including a model saying 'this is hard') cannot gate the scaffold. Count structure with code (G5).

source: Klepsch, Schmitz and Seufert (2017) Development and validation of two instruments measuring intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load, Frontiers in Psychology 8, 1997
finding: Study 1 (N=97) and Study 2 (65 to 95 per task) built questionnaires for the three loads. A three-factor model fit; intrinsic and extraneous items were reliable; germane items were weak. Trained 'informed' ratings of designed high and low element-interactivity scenarios separated well but are costly.
numbers: Study 2 fit: TLI >= .95, CFI >= .95, RMSEA <= .05. Mean Cronbach alpha for the improved items 0.81 (reliability generalization). Alpha for the three-item germane scale was not sufficient.
limits: Self-report in university learners. Germane load is hard to measure on its own. Scenario-based, not tied to a count of elements.
agent_relevance: The only reliable-looking human measure of intrinsic load is self-report. Gives no direct count; do not copy it to an agent.

source: Kaiser, Frigessi, Ramezani-Kebrya and Ricaud (2025) CogniLoad: a synthetic natural language reasoning benchmark with tunable length, intrinsic difficulty and distractor density, arXiv 2509.18458
finding: Puzzle generator with three separate knobs. Intrinsic difficulty d sets people, attributes and values and conditions per statement (element interactivity). Length N and needle-to-hay ratio set the other two. 22 reasoning LLMs. Accuracy fell as d rose for most models, but length N was the dominant stressor.
numbers: d in {1,3,5,7,10}; N in {20,50,100,250}. 13 open models x 100 puzzles per cell (14,000 each); Gemini-2.5, gpt-5, DeepSeek-R1 x 10 per cell. By d=5, 12 of 22 models were below 50%. gpt-5 0.82 and o3 0.80 at d=10. d=1 to 3: o3 0.96 to 0.93, gpt-5 1.00 to 0.97; small models lost 0.10 to 0.25. Length 20 to 50: DS-Llama-70B 0.89 to 0.66, Qwen3-8B 0.71 to 0.40.
limits: Preprint under review. Puzzle difficulty is built from entity and rule counts that the authors call element interactivity; it is not independently verified as interactivity. Context cap 32K.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of the idea. Both d and N hurt every model; N hurts most. So splitting a task into short steps cuts length but not interactivity inside each step.

source: CogniLoad (2509.18458): capacity thresholds and failure types
finding: A logistic regression gives each model a 50%-accuracy point on each knob. The main failure under load is wrong final state tracking (valid-logic errors), and small models drift to non-answers at long N.
numbers: Frontier class (gpt-5, o3) had ECL50 above 300 statements. Weak class (DS-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B) never reached 50% even at mean load. At N=250 DS-Qwen-1.5B had 605 'other' cases and DS-Qwen-7B had 461. Gemini-2.5-flash had 280 context-limit errors in 350 samples at N=250; gemini-2.5-pro 268/350; gpt-5 32/350.
limits: Per-model thresholds are fits at mean values of the other knobs, so they depend on the grid.
agent_relevance: Gives a method for the agent: measure each model's own ID50 (largest interacting set it can handle) and size sub-problems to that number rather than a fixed rule.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Beyond Accuracy: a cognitive load framework for mapping the capability boundaries of tool-use agents, arXiv 2601.20412 (AAAI 2026)
finding: Intrinsic load of a tool-use task is computed from a Tool Interaction Graph: sum over dependency edges of (turns between producer and consumer) x (1 + lambda x same-type distractors). Success per step is modeled as exp(-(k x load + b)). Fits held for 9 models on 500 tasks.
numbers: ToolLoad-Bench: 500 tasks, 10 domains, 106 tools, 4.9 calls on average (BFCL v3 base had 200 tasks, 4.1 calls). Accuracy: xLAM2-32B 78.8, GPT-4o 68.0, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 64.8, GPT-4o-mini 62.2, Gemini 2.5 Pro 60.0, Qwen3-235B 58.0, Qwen3-32B 55.2, Qwen3-8B 38.6, Llama3.3-70B 17. Fitted k (b): xLAM2 0.034 (1.22), GPT-4o 0.067 (1.71), Claude 0.073 (1.57), Qwen3-8B 0.085 (1.12). Hosmer-Lemeshow p-values all above .05.
limits: One benchmark built on BFCL. Extraneous load is rated by Gemini-2.5-pro. Independent steps assumed (Postulate 2). The lambda weight is a free hyperparameter. A non-significant H-L test shows no detected miscalibration, not proof of a good model.
agent_relevance: A usable code-computable score for S0. Count dependencies and how far apart producer and consumer are, plus look-alike distractors. Both are checkable without asking a model.

source: Shang et al. (2026) United Minds or Isolated Agents? CoThinker, TMLR; arXiv 2506.06843
finding: Uses CLT as a design lens. Pilot: attention entropy rises with task difficulty. Hard tasks gain from complex instructions, easy tasks do not. CoThinker splits intrinsic load across specialist agents. Gains concentrate on reasoning-heavy tasks and it loses on instruction-following.
numbers: Attention entropy by arithmetic level: 4.44, 4.80, 5.04. Perplexity on hard tasks by instruction level: 120.50, 88.97, 85.35; easy tasks 3.37, 3.42, 3.45. LiveBench (Gemini-1.5-Pro): Math IO 60.9 vs CoThinker 75.3; Data 40.7 vs 47.3; Reasoning 43.0 vs 44.7; Language 37.4 vs 52.6; Instruction-following 84.4 vs 81.8.
limits: The proxy links (entropy, perplexity) are the authors' own and they say it is an analogy, not proof. Only Gemini family on the main table. Multi-agent debate baselines (MAD, DMAD) scored lower on most tasks, but the gain may come from the structured load split rather than from agents arguing.
agent_relevance: Same split as our gate: helps when interactivity is high, hurts when low (instruction-following dropped 2.6 points). Supports using the scaffold only on hard items (G12), though the multi-agent part is not what we use.

source: Zhang (2025) Cognitive Load-Aware Inference (CLAI), arXiv 2507.00653
finding: Prompt-only method: model estimates the problem's intrinsic load, decomposes, cuts extraneous context, then spends tokens on reasoning. Reports about 35 percent fewer tokens at the same accuracy on GSM8K and MATH.
numbers: Llama-3-70B: GSM8K 92.5 (485 tokens) vs 92.3 (310), 36.1 percent fewer; MATH 53.9 (812) vs 53.5 (525), 35.3 percent fewer. Up to 45 percent token reduction claimed across tasks.
limits: Single author, preprint, no confidence intervals or seeds shown, and the ICL estimate is a heuristic the model produces itself. Tidy gains and model-judged load go against G5 and G10. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Not evidence that a self-rated load estimate works. The load estimate should come from code.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The illusion of thinking, arXiv 2506.06941
finding: On controlled puzzles (Tower of Hanoi, Checker Jumping, River Crossing, Blocks World) three regimes appear. At low complexity non-thinking models match or beat thinking models. At medium complexity thinking helps. At high complexity both collapse to near zero, and thinking tokens fall as the collapse nears.
numbers: Complexity set by N (disks, checkers, blocks). Models: Claude-3.7-Sonnet with and without thinking, DeepSeek-R1 vs V3, o3-mini, QwQ-32B. 25 samples per model and complexity. Accuracy goes to near zero beyond a model-specific N.
limits: Complexity here is solution length and depth (Hanoi needs 2^N - 1 moves), not element interactivity, so it measures a different axis. The paper's claims were disputed in follow-up comments on output limits; I did not open those.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 and G12: do not think long on easy items, and do not expect more thinking to rescue items past the model's limit. Decompose before the limit.

source: Dziri et al. (2023) Faith and fate: limits of transformers on compositionality, NeurIPS; arXiv 2305.18654
finding: Tasks as computation graphs (multiplication, logic grid puzzles, dynamic programming). Zero-shot accuracy falls toward zero as depth and width grow, and falls with average parallelism. Fine-tuning on all small cases still fails out of distribution on deeper or wider graphs.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 reached 55 percent and 59 percent on 3-digit by 3-digit multiplication. 82.3 percent of correct answers for 4-digit by 2-digit multiplication had at least one wrong node in the computation graph. 1.8M multiplication pairs, 142K DP pairs, 41K puzzle pairs used for fine-tuning GPT-3.
limits: Older models (GPT-3 to GPT-4). Authors say the pattern is subgraph matching, not systematic reasoning. Width (parallel steps) and depth are both varied, so interactivity is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Width and parallelism correlate with error, matching the interaction idea. Single steps are near perfect; composing many is where it breaks. Check each node of the plan, not only the final answer (G2, G3).

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models, ICLR; arXiv 2205.10625
finding: Decomposition into sub-questions solved in order, each fed the earlier answers. On the SCAN length split, least-to-most reached 99.7 percent against 16.2 percent for chain of thought with the same model.
numbers: code-davinci-002 on SCAN length split: standard prompting 16.7, chain of thought 16.2, least-to-most 99.7.
limits: SCAN is a synthetic grammar task with a clean decomposition. The gain shows where the split is easy to specify; on real tasks the decomposition itself can be wrong.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct match to O3: split until each part is small, then chain. It works when the decomposition is known; the open question is making a good split on messy items.

source: Fesser, Ektefaie, Fang, Kakade and Zitnik (2026) Evaluating relational reasoning in LLMs with REL, ICML (PMLR 306); arXiv 2604.12176
finding: Builds on Halford's relational complexity (RC): the number of entities that must be bound at once. Holding entity count and input size fixed, accuracy of frontier models falls steadily as RC rises. More test-time compute and one-shot examples did not remove the drop.
numbers: RPM and tensors: accuracy drops 45 percent when RC goes 3 to 9. Phylogeny task REL-B1: RC 5 to 20 gives a 93 percent fall. Chemistry: completion rate falls 39.7 percent from REL-C1 to C3. RC=1 and 2 solved nearly perfectly, up to 91 percent on 30x30 grids. Tokens 4K, 8K, 16K changed completion by 0.4 percent on average. One-shot added 6.6, 3.4, 6.0 points (C1,C2,C3) but kept the order. RC explained 24 percent (Claude), 32 percent (Gemini), 44 percent (GPT) of explainable variance in REL-B1.
limits: Three frontier models (Claude, Gemini, GPT-5.2). RC is assigned by the authors. Larger inputs sometimes raise RC too, which they try to separate. Tool use (RDKit) did not fix REL-C3 (recall 0.094).
agent_relevance: Best single piece of 2026 evidence that the interacting-set size, not length, is what breaks models, and that extra thinking does not fix it. This justifies a decomposition gate that counts arity.

source: CogniLoad and REL both cite Halford et al. (1998) as the formal basis
finding: Two 2025-26 LLM papers (CogniLoad, REL) cite Halford et al. (1998), not Sweller, as the formal basis for intrinsic load. Sweller 1994 gives only a rough count.
numbers: CogniLoad d scaling: state space (d+1)^d; people max(d,2); attributes d; values max(d+1,3); up to d conditions per statement.
limits: Citation pattern seen in two papers only. CogniLoad's mapping from d to interactivity is by design, not validated against a human measure.
agent_relevance: If the gate is built, use arity (Halford) as the measure and cite Sweller for the effect.
